spot.v: Fog so dense the shelves are barely visible, a hand held in the stream gets wet, yellow caps and weekly 'I have blotch' calls. Ordinary hygrometers cannot read coarse fog.

look.v: Fine high-pressure mist leaves a hand dry.

cause.v: Ultrasonic units and fogger drums INSIDE the room recirculate spores and dirt through a warm water vat. A pond fogger drum is most linked to blotch complaints.
Cycle timers (30 on, 10 off) are the wrong way to control humidity.

treat.v: Box the unit in a corner with a vent through an outside wall, so it draws outside air. Dose bleach 150-250 ppm by peristaltic pump. Clean often.

prevent.v: Best to worst: high-pressure fine fog, steam, ultrasonic outside the room, compressor misting heads, pond fogger drum, anything inside the room.
One farm cured chronic blotch with a Hart high-pressure system after biocide sprays failed.

name: UNTREATED WATER
aka: MICROBES AND MINERALS IN HUMIDIFIER WATER

spot.v: Blotch or rose comb in your room, while a block of the same batch fruits fine on a kitchen counter. Fruit colour changes when minerals in hydration water are untreated.

look.v: Spawn or block-supplier faults show during incubation and across a lot, not only at fruiting.

cause.v: Sediment and microbes in humidifier water reach the fruit through the air. A shallow dug well carries more microbes than a drilled well of about 200 ft (61 m). Deep wells in drought areas can carry bacterial blooms and heavy minerals.
Water used to hydrate substrate that is then cooked rarely causes problems.

treat.v: Chain: particulate filter, softener if hard, carbon, then RO or steam for the fruit line. Inline UV (sized in gal/h) is the cheap first line, mainly worth it on wells. Add bleach 150-250 ppm or ClO2 dosing.
Example for a shallow mineral-rich coastal well, worked out with Cap n Stem: 1000 micron spin-down, 100 and 50 micron, sediment, iron filter, carbon, UV; softener for boiler feed; DI/RO for misting.

prevent.v: Use multiple barriers. Do not use Lysol, Pine-Sol or vinegar in fogger water.

risk.v: Any fruiting species; oysters show it first.

spot.v: Water pooled on fruit-room floors, in flutes of wall sheets, or in drains without traps.

cause.v: Standing water breeds bacterial blooms. Sewer or septic air backs up through untrapped drains and brings bacteria, including blotch.

treat.v: Vacuum it out, push wash water to the drain, leave no standing water.

prevent.v: Floor drains with P-traps in fruit rooms. Smooth, washable walls.

spot.v: Mycelium growing out of caps in cold weather. Worse: bacteria and even rose comb.

look.v: A small cap growing on a cap on chestnut is usually harmless.

cause.v: Cold air holds less moisture, so humidity output that was right in summer condenses on fruit in winter.

treat.v: Finer atomization (high-pressure fog nozzles). Stop the condensation.

prevent.v: Match humidity output to the season; swing humidity 70-90%.

spot.v: Spores clog ductwork in humid air and foul cooler fins and coils. Opening a full shiitake room released a cloud that broke a fan.

look.v: Blotch and mould are living contaminants; this is the crop's own spore load.

cause.v: Overblown mushrooms shed more spores. Recirculating coolers and humidifiers in a spore-laden space clog and spread it.

treat.v: Clean the room daily if possible: about 250 ppm bleach, power wash or wipe, push water to the drain. Keep a backup fan.

prevent.v: Harvest on time. Keep coolers out of the plenum and away from fruit rooms. Isopropyl foot baths make little difference.

risk.v: Shiitake named; maitake may do the same (unconfirmed).
